A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Human Simulacra dataset, MACM framework, and psychology-guided evaluation. Their text, tables, figures, and equations support reliable comparison. v5 has no appendix; v6's Appendices A-H are available and readable.

before.justification: v5 reports original self-report evaluations across LLMs, human-judged observer evaluations, and dialogue case studies in Section 6, Tables 2-3, and Figure 5.

after.justification: v6 retains original self-report and observer evaluations and adds conformity simulations, component ablations, and character-diversity analysis in Section 5 and Appendices A, B, and E.

M1.justification: The character-generation pipeline, Jung-based personality modeling, and four-agent MACM retain their procedures. v5 Section 4 matches v6 Section 4.3 and Appendix B: memory construction, retrieval, logical/emotional analysis, and response aggregation remain. The new pseudocode and prompts disclose implementation details rather than establish an algorithmic revision.

E1.justification: The same 11-character Human Simulacra dataset remains, but v6 adds an Asch-style conformity task requiring decisions under group pressure and subsequent interviews (Section 5.2, Appendix E). Table 12 also introduces conflicting multi-turn interactions. These extend evaluation beyond the earlier self-report, observer-report, and isolated dialogue scenarios.

E2.justification: The existing None, Prompt, and RAG comparison methods remain. v6 adds a Human reference row to Table 2 and compares MACM with Character.ai and published human results in the conformity experiment (Figure 7). Character-LLM and Role-LLM appear in a descriptive dataset comparison, not as newly evaluated experimental baselines.

E3.justification: v6 expands the ten-model evaluation to fourteen models by adding three Claude-3 variants and Qwen-turbo. Its new conformity protocol uses 18 trials, including 12 critical trials, across 11 characters, followed by interviews; Table 28 supplies numerical line lengths through text prompts. Component-removal experiments introduce additional controls. Existing evaluation scores are also rescaled from 50 to 100 points.

E4.justification: v6 adds agent-removal and memory-source ablations across three LLMs (Table 4), character-diversity analysis (Appendix A.3), a worked retrieval/reasoning example (Table 10), and a conflicting multi-turn case (Table 12). Appendix E analyzes conformity across models and simulation methods. The earlier Mary Jones dialogue examples largely reappear in Table 11 and are not new analyses.

E5.justification: v6 Table 3 first reports inter-judge intraclass correlations: 0.86 for description matching and 0.95 for response similarity. Both versions retain three repeated self-report tests and majority-selected dialogue examples from three tests. No increase in repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance testing is established.

E6.justification: v6 adds four model rows, previously missing MACM results for Llama-2-70b and Llama-2-70b-Chat (56.00 and 58.66), and ablation, conformity, and dialogue findings. Shared Table 2 scores are equivalent after rescaling and rounding. Some Table 3 entries change beyond rescaling: Prompt's total changes from 34.63/50 to 69.00/100. Figure 12 also exchanges James's and Kevin's reported story lengths relative to v5 Table 1.

T1.justification: Appendix A.3 newly defines inter-character distance as d_total = (d_L1 + 1 - tau)/2, combining normalized attribute distance and personality-ranking similarity. v5 has no equivalent definition. The cognitive-psychology foundations remain, and no new theorem or proof is introduced.

C1.justification: The central dataset, MACM, two-part evaluation, and character-alignment claims remain. v6 adds an explicit novelty claim for Jung-based human-simulation data and standard simulation experiments, and highlights personality-dependent but rigid conformity as a main finding. These extend the contribution claims without replacing the original research proposition.

C2.justification: v6 interprets conformity results as exposing rigid personalities that fail to reproduce changing human responses. Section 6 and Appendix A add substantive discussion of Jung's limited empirical support, omitted nationality/race attributes, target selection, and the cost-constrained dataset size. Conversely, v5's explicit warning that the proposed approach inherits adversarial vulnerabilities is not retained as a comparable limitation.

D1.justification: v6 adds construction pseudocode and scoring weights, attribute-sampling rules, retrieval details, questionnaires, judge rubrics, full prompts, and hardware/cost information (Appendices A, D, F, and G). Its reproducibility statement supplies a code/data access link, replacing v5's future-release promise. These substantially expand documentation; they do not establish changes to the underlying implementation. v5's option-shuffling detail is no longer documented.

R1.justification: v6 substantially expands positioning beyond v5's memory-systems discussion and brief role-playing comparisons. It adds a dedicated role-playing discussion and dataset comparison table, engages work such as Generative Agents and critiques of LLM personality self-assessment, and develops comparisons among personality theories. Asch-related literature also supports the newly introduced psychological application.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten. MACM moves from a standalone section into the evaluation framework with details in Appendix B; qualitative analysis moves to Appendix C. Dataset-generation subsections are merged, and a substantial Discussion, reproducibility statement, and organized appendices replace the earlier compact structure and standalone limitations/ethics treatment.

P2.justification: v6 changes to a single-column conference layout and substantially redesigns the visual presentation. It combines the earlier information-chain and generation diagrams, expands the evaluation and MACM diagrams, presents character information through cards and charts, and converts the earlier dialogue figure into Table 11. New conformity figures, ablation tables, ICC columns, and extensive appendix displays further change presentation.

improvement.justification: v6 addresses important weaknesses in v5: missing component-level validation and insufficient detail to reproduce the method and human evaluation. Table 4's ablations, the full prompts and judge rubrics, and agreement statistics substantially strengthen assessability. The conformity study also exposes a concrete behavioral limitation. These gains outweigh remaining problems, including limited comparability with human visual trials and the introductory observer score of 77.75% conflicting with Table 3's 77.50.
